clue.text: Woman out of staff college goes into fighting force

indicators.note: the college's letters go into the woman's name, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Ada is a woman's name
RMA, the Royal Military Academy, which trains army officers

explanation.surface: A woman leaves an officers' college to join the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' just joins: the woman is from the college. The college abbreviation RMA goes into ADA.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish fleet sent against England, this word now means any large war fleet or force.

clue.text: Graduate delving into poet, mostly early composition

indicators.note: the degree delves into, goes inside, the shortened poet
most of the poet's name, its last letter dropped

parts.note: W H Auden was an English poet
BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: A graduate researching a poet finds an early work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'early' looks like 'youthful', as if the poet's juvenilia, but here it means of the dawn: the song is sung at daybreak.
explanation.definitionFit: A song or poem greeting the dawn, so a composition for the early morning.

clue.text: As men play game of cricket, it may lead to a benefit

definitions.text: it may lead to a benefit

indicators.note: play suggests the letters frolicking into a new order

parts.note: a Test match is an international cricket game

explanation.surface: Men playing a Test match hope for a benefit match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'play' turns AS MEN into MEANS. Cricketers get benefit matches, misleading from welfare benefits.
explanation.definitionFit: A check on a person's income decides whether they qualify for state welfare payments.

clue.text: The informal look

parts.note: a slang word for having a look, borrowed from Hindi by British soldiers

explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a quick look, from the Hindi word for see.

clue.text: Malicious fuel-spill on narrow stretch of coast

indicators.note: in this clue the shuffled fuel comes on, or after, the stretch of coast

parts.note: a spit is a narrow point of land running out into the sea

indicators.note: fuel that spills is thrown about, so its four letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone spitefully spills fuel along a sandy spit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'fuel-spill' as one noun, an oil slick on the coast; in fact 'spill' is the signal to jumble the four letters before them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone who wants to hurt or upset others out of ill will.

clue.text: Losing one's head? Spaniard loses his

indicators.note: the Spaniard loses some letters, which are taken out

parts.note: a Spaniard is Hispanic
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Spaniard panics and loses his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing one's head' is the definition; 'his' is taken literally from HISPANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing one's head means losing composure, which is giving way to sudden fear.

clue.text: Boss, maybe the best, given a hand?

parts.note: top means the best
a hand is a bunch of bananas, each fruit a finger

explanation.surface: A boss, perhaps the best of them, gets a round of applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given a hand' looks like applause, but bananas grow in clusters called hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for the person in charge, the chief.

clue.text: Instant type of photography

definitions.meaning: a moment, as in in a split second
photography using a sudden burst of light

explanation.surface: A kind of camera work done in a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A split second, and photography lit by a sudden burst of light.

clue.text: Willing to have dressing round tissue

indicators.note: the dressing goes round the word for willing

parts.note: lint is a fabric used to dress wounds
game means willing, up for it

explanation.surface: A willing patient has a bandage put round damaged tissue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to have' just joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Fibrous connective tissue binding bones together at a joint.

clue.text: What Mikado threatened billiard cheat with, we hear, in a decorative twist

indicators.note: we hear marks a sound-alike: the spelt word is said like the phrase

parts.words: What Mikado threatened billiard cheat with
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, the billiard sharp must play with a twisted cue, a curly cue

explanation.surface: The Mikado's punishment for a cheat at billiards takes a fancy twist.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Mikado's song the billiard sharp is made to play 'on a cloth untrue, with a twisted cue'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy curl or flourish in handwriting or decoration.

clue.text: Rovers, maybe, threatening to show passion

parts.note: black clouds or looks are threatening ones
to burn with love or anger is to show passion

explanation.surface: A football team's fans look menacing in their fervour.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackburn Rovers is an English football club; 'maybe' marks the town as one example of a club name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancashire town gives its name to a football club known as the Rovers, so the town is Rovers by example.

clue.text: Run through pain, causing damage

indicators.note: the run abbreviation passes through the pain word, sitting inside it

parts.note: a pang is a sudden sharp pain
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A runner pushes on through pain and hurts himself.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for crashing a car or plane and so damaging it; the clue's phrase stands for the verb.

clue.text: Was not honest about military campaigns turning in plunder

indicators.note: the whole assembly is turned round and read backwards
the word for lying goes about, around, the campaigns

parts.note: lied means was not honest
ops is short for military operations

explanation.surface: A dishonest officer covers up looting during campaigns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' applies to the whole assembly, not just the campaigns: build the container first, then read all seven letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To despoil a place is to strip it of its valuables, which is to plunder it.

clue.text: PM has long ago entered academic stream

indicators.note: the archaic word enters, going inside, the river's name

parts.note: the Cam is the river through Cambridge
hath is the old form of has

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister of old takes a punt on a university river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Earl of Chatham was William Pitt the Elder, Prime Minister in the 1760s. 'long ago' marks the archaic HATH.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitt the Elder held the title Earl of Chatham, so the title stands for that Prime Minister.

clue.text: Terribly sensitive actor, during long run, refuelling here?

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly disordered, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A highly strung actor in a long-running show needs topping up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terribly' jumbles SENSITIVE and ACTOR together. The 'long run' looks theatrical, but it is a long drive.
explanation.definitionFit: On a long motorway journey drivers stop at a roadside services to buy fuel.

clue.text: Offence as member of musical family gets broken into

parts.note: the viola is a member of the violin family

indicators.note: the word into is broken up, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A violist's home is burgled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken into' looks like burglary, but 'broken' shuffles INTO to give TION.
explanation.definitionFit: A breach of a rule or law, which is an offence.

clue.text: On top of cases, like this old question-master?

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the other

parts.note: so means in this way
crates are cases for packing

explanation.surface: A quizmaster sits on top of some boxes.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek philosopher taught by asking questions, the Socratic method.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian thinker taught by questioning his pupils, so he was a master of questions.

clue.text: Visiting valley, took time out in warm corner

parts.note: in means visiting, at home somewhere
a glen is a Scottish valley

indicators.note: the time abbreviation is taken out of the word

explanation.surface: A walker visiting a valley takes a break by a fireside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time out' drops T from TOOK, leaving OOK.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosy seat by a large open fireplace.

clue.text: Does some waffling, with good word-play

parts.note: riddles are puzzles of word-play

explanation.surface: Someone talks nonsense but with clever puns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waffling' suggests chatter, but it means making waffles, cooked on a flat plate.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooking waffles or pancakes on a flat iron plate, which is cooking on a hotplate.

clue.text: Get it for a few pounds, by the speed one bargains?

definitions.text: Get it for a few pounds
definitions.meaning: what you are given in foreign money when you hand over some pounds sterling
read literally, the pace at which one trades or swaps

explanation.surface: A tourist asks how quickly one can haggle for currency.
explanation.definitionFit: The ratio at which pounds are swapped for foreign money, and literally the speed of trading.

clue.text: Author piling on the heat?

definitions.meaning: Bram, the Irish writer of Dracula
one who feeds a furnace with fuel

explanation.surface: A writer turning up the heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram, who wrote Dracula, shares a name with someone who feeds a furnace.

clue.text: Nonconformist's artless about probing boozer's problem

indicators.note: the reversed word probes, going inside, the drinker's complaint

parts.note: DTs, delirium tremens, afflict heavy drinkers

indicators.note: the word for artless is turned about, read backwards

parts.note: naive means artless, innocent

explanation.surface: An innocent rebel examines a drunk's troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is' joining definition to wordplay. 'Nonconformist' suggests a chapel-goer, but here it simply means someone outside the norm.
explanation.definitionFit: A deviant departs from accepted norms, which is what a nonconformist does.

clue.text: Virulent feeling against cash being raised finally going

parts.note: V is short for versus, against

indicators.note: in a down clue raising a word turns it upwards, reading backwards
the final letter of the cash word goes

parts.note: money means cash

explanation.surface: Bitterness against money-raising that has finally gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally going' cuts MONEY to MONE; 'being raised' turns it into ENOM.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiteful bitterness, likened to a snake's poison.

clue.text: Going along to shrink

parts.note: something that gets narrower bit by bit as it goes along its length, like a thin candle

explanation.definitionFit: To become gradually narrower along a length, as a spire or a slim candle does.

clue.text: Pistol so old-fashioned

definitions.meaning: Shakespeare's swaggering soldier in Henry V is styled ... Pistol, ... being an old rank of ensign

explanation.surface: A firearm described as outdated.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol is not a gun but Shakespeare's character, whose title was this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Pistol holds the rank of ensign, called by this title, and the word also means very old.

clue.text: European vet gets reported

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the word is the sound-alike of a spoken one

parts.note: to vet is to check

explanation.surface: A European vet is reported.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from the Czech Republic is a European.

clue.text: Eastern dress I put on part of body

indicators.note: the letter is put on, added after, the organ

parts.note: a lung is a part of the body

explanation.surface: Someone puts on an Eastern garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' looks like dressing, but it adds I after LUNG.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth wrapped round the waist and worn in India and South-East Asia.

clue.text: Method of payment covering two musical compositions

parts.note: a piece is a musical composition
a work is another musical composition

explanation.surface: Someone is paid for writing two pieces of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Being paid per item produced rather than by the hour is a payment method.

clue.text: House — in dialect not a college

parts.note: a semi is a semi-detached house
nary is a dialect form meaning not a, as in nary a word

explanation.surface: Someone insists, in local speech, that a building is not a college.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi, short for semi-detached, is a British house joined to its neighbour on one side.
explanation.definitionFit: A college that trains priests or ministers.

clue.text: Religious American helps make cocktails

definitions.meaning: a member of an American religious sect famous for simple furniture
a container in which cocktails are mixed

explanation.surface: A devout American mixes drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the American sect named for its ecstatic movement, and the vessel used to mix cocktails.
